newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Strained at home, China reaches out for foreign oil.
newsitem.headline: Strained at home, China reaches out for foreign oil.

text.p: Unble to expand oil resources at home fast enough to meet rapidly rising demand, China is in hot pursuit of joint ventures with foreign firms and reaching out for resources abroad, analysts said on Monday.
"There is a problem... we haven't found significant increase on our own oilfields," said a well-placed source with state importer China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec).
China's proven oil reserves are around 16.9 billion barrels (2.3 billion tonnes), according to Chinese state media.
Kang Wu, an energy specialist at the Hawaii-based East-West Centre, predicted China's oil production would continue to grow in the next 15 years, but at a slow pace.
Chinese officials say they expected China to import 50 million tonnes by the year 2000, compared with 22.6 million in 1996, and analysts are estimating 74 million tonnes by 2005.
For China, the best partners are in the Middle East such as Iran and Iraq because they have the resources and are seen as with less threats to China, analysts said.

"China must link with foreign firms to develop oilfields at home because it does need foreign funds, but there are worries that foreign firms will share the cake in Chinese oilfields," said a U.S.-based energy analyst.
"So the idea is to slowly allow foreign firms to step into China with funds but at the same time it agressively looks for foreign oil," he said.

Speeding up exploration in remote oilfields such as in northwestern Xinjiang will be expensive for budget-tight China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC), the state's onshore oil exploration and production firm, analysts said.
"It's not economic to spend a huge amount of money under bad conditions in remote deserts, dig out oil reserves then transport the oil to the south," the U.S.-based analyst said.
China's oil-rich Xinjinag province is in the far west, while most demand comes from the booming southeast coast.
"It makes much more sense to get cheaper oil from foreign countries," the analyst said.
Apart from geographic difficulties, analysts said funding exploration was also a main concern for the CNPC, which has some 1.5 million employees.
"Of course it's better to replace all aged equipment, but the problem is there is not enough money," said a CNPC source who declined to be named.
So the state explorer reaches out.
In the latest of several such announcements, CNPC and Iran agreed last Tuesday to form a joint venture to explore for offshore oil and gas in Iran, China and in third countries.
Just one week before that, CNPC and Italy's Agip SpA agreed to form a joint oil venture to operate in areas of common interest worldwide in exploration, production, refining, distribution and sales.
That followed a $1.2-billion development of a field in southern Iraq and a $3.5-billion pact with Kazakhstan for a 3,000-km pipeline to China's Xinjiang.
In the same week, China also signed two 20-year contracts to operate and expand oilfields in Venezuela.
"China's current policy is to make the best use of international resources," said Hu Angang, an energy analyst at Chinese Academy of Science in Beijing.
"China will be even more active in international markets because there is not so much oil at home," Hu said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703571)
